Title: How to Review PRs Like a Maintainer
Desc: Learn how experienced maintainers review pull requests, spot potential issues early, provide useful feedback, and keep software projects healthy without slowing down development.
Author: M Ramzan Ch
Data:
Many developers think a pull request review means one thing:

```text
Read Code
↓
Approve
```

In reality, experienced maintainers approach reviews very differently.

A good review isn't just about finding bugs.

It's about ensuring:

* Code quality
* Maintainability
* Security
* Consistency
* Long-term project health

The best maintainers review code with future contributors and future users in mind.

Let's explore how they do it.

---

## What Is a Pull Request Review?

A pull request (PR) review is the process of evaluating proposed code changes before merging them into the main codebase.

The goal is not to criticize contributors.

The goal is:

```text id="review-goal"
Improve The Code
Not Win Arguments
```

A successful review helps both the project and the contributor.

---

## Think Like a Maintainer, Not a Tester

New reviewers often focus only on:

```text id="bug-focus"
Does It Work?
```

Maintainers ask additional questions:

* Will this be easy to maintain?
* Does it fit the project's architecture?
* Is it consistent with existing patterns?
* Will future developers understand it?

Working code is important.

Maintainable code is equally important.

## Start With the Big Picture

Before reading individual lines, understand:

### What Problem Is Being Solved?

Read:

* PR title
* Description
* Linked issue
* Related discussions

Ask:

```text id="problem-check"
Does This Change Solve The Right Problem?
```

Sometimes the implementation is excellent but addresses the wrong issue.

---

## Review the Overall Approach First

Don't immediately focus on syntax.

Instead evaluate:

* Architecture
* Design decisions
* Data flow
* System impact

Process:

```text id="review-process"
Problem
↓
Approach
↓
Implementation
↓
Details
```

Maintainers review from top to bottom.

---

## Check Scope Creep

A common PR problem:

```text id="scope-creep"
Fix Bug
+
Refactor Components
+
Update Dependencies
+
Change Styling
```

One PR becomes four projects.

Large mixed changes are difficult to review.

Prefer focused pull requests.

---

## Read the Code Like a New Contributor

Ask yourself:

```text id="new-dev"
Would A New Developer Understand This?
```

Look for:

* Clear naming
* Readable logic
* Helpful comments
* Consistent structure

If code is confusing today, it will be confusing six months from now.

---

![Software engineering code review process](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1516321318423-f06f85e504b3)

## Look for Maintainability

Maintainers often prioritize maintainability over cleverness.

Example:

Less maintainable:

```javascript id="complex-example"
const r=a.filter(x=>x.p&&x.s).map(x=>x.v)
```

More maintainable:

```javascript id="clear-example"
const activeUsers = users
  .filter(user => user.isPublished)
  .map(user => user.value)
```

Readable code usually wins.

---

## Check for Consistency

Every project develops patterns.

Review whether the contribution follows:

* Naming conventions
* Folder structure
* Architecture decisions
* Coding style

Consistency reduces cognitive load.

---

## Verify Tests

Ask:

```text id="test-question"
How Do We Know This Works?
```

Look for:

* Unit tests
* Integration tests
* Regression tests

Changes without testing deserve extra scrutiny.

---

## Review Error Handling

Happy paths are easy.

Maintainers also check:

* Invalid input
* Failed requests
* Missing data
* Unexpected behavior

Example:

```text id="error-flow"
Success
↓
Failure
↓
Recovery
```

Reliable software handles all three.

---

![Developer testing software changes](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1515879218367-8466d910aaa4)

## Consider Performance

Not every change requires optimization.

But reviewers should ask:

* Does this increase database queries?
* Does this add expensive operations?
* Does it affect page load times?

Small inefficiencies can become major issues at scale.

---

## Think About Security

Even small changes can create security risks.

Review:

* User input handling
* Authentication logic
* Authorization checks
* Sensitive data exposure

Question:

```text id="security-check"
Could This Be Abused?
```

Maintainers ask this often.

---

## Check Documentation

Code changes may require documentation updates.

Examples:

* New features
* Configuration changes
* API modifications
* Breaking changes

Documentation is part of the product.

---

## Leave Constructive Feedback

Bad review:

```text id="bad-feedback"
This Is Wrong.
```

Better review:

```text id="good-feedback"
Could we use the existing helper function here to stay consistent with the rest of the codebase?
```

Constructive feedback improves collaboration.

---

## Explain Why

Experienced maintainers explain reasoning.

Example:

```text id="explain-why"
This approach may cause duplicate database queries under heavy traffic.
```

Context helps contributors learn.

---

![Collaborative software development and feedback](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1517048676732-d65bc937f952)

## Avoid Nitpicking Everything

Not every issue deserves a blocking comment.

Separate feedback into:

### Critical

Must fix before merging.

---

### Suggested

Improvement ideas.

---

### Optional

Personal preferences.

This keeps reviews focused.

---

## Review the User Experience

Maintainers don't only review code.

They also review outcomes.

Ask:

* Is the feature intuitive?
* Does it improve usability?
* Could it confuse users?

Users care about results, not implementation details.

---

## Watch for Technical Debt

Questions to ask:

* Does this create future maintenance work?
* Does it duplicate existing functionality?
* Is there a cleaner solution?

Technical debt compounds over time.

---

## Common PR Review Mistakes

### Reviewing Too Quickly

Fast approvals can miss serious issues.

---

### Focusing Only on Style

Formatting matters, but architecture matters more.

---

### Ignoring Tests

Untested code creates risk.

---

### Making Reviews Personal

Reviews should focus on code, not people.

---

### Blocking Every Minor Issue

Not every suggestion needs to delay a merge.

---

## A Maintainer's Review Checklist

Before approving a PR, verify:

* [ ] Problem is understood
* [ ] Solution makes sense
* [ ] Scope is appropriate
* [ ] Code is readable
* [ ] Tests exist
* [ ] Error handling is adequate
* [ ] Security concerns addressed
* [ ] Performance impact considered
* [ ] Documentation updated
* [ ] Feedback communicated clearly

This simple checklist catches many issues.

---

## Example Review Workflow

A practical review process:

```text id="workflow"
Read Description
↓
Understand Problem
↓
Review Architecture
↓
Review Code
↓
Check Tests
↓
Check Documentation
↓
Provide Feedback
↓
Approve Or Request Changes
```

Maintainers typically follow a similar pattern.

---

## FAQ

### What should I review first in a PR?

Start with understanding the problem being solved before examining implementation details.

### How detailed should PR reviews be?

Detailed enough to ensure quality, but focused on meaningful issues rather than personal preferences.

### Should every PR have tests?

Ideally yes, especially for new features, bug fixes, and critical functionality.

### How do maintainers give feedback?

Constructively, clearly, and with explanations that help contributors learn.

### What is the biggest mistake in PR reviews?

Focusing on small style issues while ignoring architecture, maintainability, or testing concerns.

---

## Final Thoughts

Great pull request reviews are not about proving expertise or finding every tiny flaw. They're about helping projects remain healthy, maintainable, and reliable over time.

Experienced maintainers review code from a long-term perspective. They evaluate architecture before syntax, maintainability before cleverness, and collaboration before criticism.

The next time you review a PR, think beyond whether the code works today. Consider whether the project will still benefit from that code a year from now.

That's how maintainers review pull requests.
